questions.stem: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) occurs when:

choices.A: User-controllable identifiers access resources without per-object authorisation checks
choices.B: SQL injection accesses database objects directly
choices.C: A user directly executes server-side scripts
choices.D: An API exposes internal schemas in error messages

questions.explanation: IDOR lets attackers access arbitrary resources by manipulating an ID parameter without the server verifying per-object authorisation.

choices.A: Accessing another user's data at the same privilege level
choices.B: Exploiting a service running with elevated permissions
choices.C: A lower-privileged user gaining higher-privileged (e.g., admin) access
choices.D: Moving from one system to another with equivalent access

questions.explanation: Vertical escalation moves up the privilege hierarchy, user to admin. Horizontal escalation accesses another user's resources at the same level.

questions.stem: Function-level access checks must be implemented:

choices.A: Client-side only to reduce server load
choices.B: Based on URL path only without authentication context
choices.D: Server-side for every sensitive function regardless of whether the UI presents the option

questions.explanation: Client-side controls (hidden buttons, disabled menus) are trivially bypassed by direct API calls. Server-side authorisation must validate every request.

choices.B: Authenticating users with username and password
choices.C: Delegated authorisation, allowing third-party apps to access resources on behalf of users without sharing credentials

questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 is an authorisation delegation framework enabling users to grant third-party apps limited access without sharing actual credentials.

choices.A: The authenticated user lacks permission for the specific resource or action
choices.D: The requested resource does not exist

questions.explanation: 403 Forbidden means the server understands the request and the user is authenticated, but lacks authorisation. 401 means authentication failed.

choices.A: Encrypted and unreadable without the server's private key
choices.C: Base64URL-encoded and directly readable by anyone, the signature prevents tampering, not reading
choices.D: Only readable after successful HMAC verification

questions.explanation: JWT payload is Base64URL-encoded, not encrypted. Any decoder immediately reads the claims. The signature verifies integrity but conceals nothing.

questions.stem: Rate limiting on an API primarily protects against:

choices.D: Credential brute-force, IDOR enumeration, and denial of service through excessive requests

questions.explanation: Rate limiting caps requests per source per time window, making brute-force attacks, sequential IDOR enumeration, and resource exhaustion impractical.

questions.stem: The JWT 'none' algorithm vulnerability allows attackers to:

choices.B: Forge signatures using a weak algorithm
choices.C: Set alg=none and remove the signature, bypassing verification on vulnerable libraries

questions.explanation: Some JWT libraries accept 'alg: none' as valid without requiring a signature. Attackers modify the algorithm to 'none' and strip the signature to forge tokens.

questions.stem: Broken Access Control is OWASP #1 because:

choices.A: It is the most technically complex exploit
choices.B: It always results in remote code execution
choices.C: Access control failures appear in many forms and are found in a large proportion of tested applications

questions.explanation: Broken access control is #1 because it manifests in many forms (IDOR, privilege escalation, force browsing) and is found in the vast majority of tested applications.

choices.A: Organisational roles that users are then assigned to

questions.explanation: RBAC assigns permissions to roles. Users inherit permissions through role assignment, simplifying access management in large organisations.
